texts.orig: Eye Health: Dry Eye with Diabetes
texts.text: Eye Health: Dry Eye with Diabetes

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One of the most common, yet rarely talked about, eye conditions in people with diabetes is dry eye. Studies have shown 54 percent of people with diabetes have dry eye.
texts.text: One of the most common, yet rarely talked about, eye conditions in people with diabetes is dry eye. Studies have shown 54 percent of people with diabetes have dry eye.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Also known as dry eye syndrome (DES), dry eye disease, or keratoconjunctivitis sicca , this condition sounds harmless but should be taken just as seriously as any other diabetes eye complication. In fact, they are often related. Quite literally, DES is characterized by a lack of fluid on and around the surface of your eye or poor quality of tears on the front surface of the eye. The causes vary and there is more than a dozen recognized types of dry eye, and each may require different treatment strategies.
texts.text: Also known as dry eye syndrome (DES), dry eye disease, or keratoconjunctivitis sicca , this condition sounds harmless but should be taken just as seriously as any other diabetes eye complication. In fact, they are often related. Quite literally, DES is characterized by a lack of fluid on and around the surface of your eye or poor quality of tears on the front surface of the eye. The causes vary and there is more than a dozen recognized types of dry eye, and each may require different treatment strategies.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Healthy eyes require constant production of tears to maintain their moisture. Crying leads to the production of more tears. And you've likely experienced your eyes watering excessively when something is irritating them.
texts.text: Healthy eyes require constant production of tears to maintain their moisture. Crying leads to the production of more tears. And you've likely experienced your eyes watering excessively when something is irritating them.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Tears are made of three ingredients-water, oil, and mucus-that keep the surface of your eyes clear, smooth, and capable of seeing clearly. when you aren't producing enough tears long-term, it can lead to DES.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Why Diabetes Increases Your Risk of DES
texts.text: Why Diabetes Increases Your Risk of DES

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You likely already know that diabetes-and more specifically, chronically high blood glucose (blood sugar)- can create many complications in your eyes, including retinopathy, cataracts, and glaucoma. In short, there are several ways diabetes causes dry eyes. Diabetes affects the function of the lacrimal gland, which produces watery parts of your tears. Diabetes also affects oil glands in our eyelids that prevent the watery part of our tears from evaporating too quickly after each blink. These glands are responsible for producing tears and maintaining healthy moisture levels in your eyes.
texts.text: You likely already know that diabetes-and more specifically, chronically high blood glucose (blood sugar)- can create many complications in your eyes, including retinopathy, cataracts, and glaucoma. In short, there are several ways diabetes causes dry eyes. Diabetes affects the function of the lacrimal gland, which produces watery parts of your tears. Diabetes also affects oil glands in our eyelids that prevent the watery part of our tears from evaporating too quickly after each blink. These glands are responsible for producing tears and maintaining healthy moisture levels in your eyes.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig:  Insulin plays a critical role in the function of the lacrimal gland. Inadequate insulin levels in the body can lead to decreased tear production.
texts.text:  Insulin plays a critical role in the function of the lacrimal gland. Inadequate insulin levels in the body can lead to decreased tear production.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig:  High blood glucose can damage nerves throughout your eyes, including the nerves in the lacrimal gland and nerves on the eyes clear window, called the cornea. These nerves are necessary for tears to 'stick' to the front surface of the eye. This means overall blood flow to this area becomes limited, leading to decreased tear production (quantity of tears) as well as decreased tear adhesion to the eye (quality of tears).
texts.text:  High blood glucose can damage nerves throughout your eyes, including the nerves in the lacrimal gland and nerves on the eyes clear window, called the cornea. These nerves are necessary for tears to 'stick' to the front surface of the eye. This means overall blood flow to this area becomes limited, leading to decreased tear production (quantity of tears) as well as decreased tear adhesion to the eye (quality of tears).

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig:  Inflammation and immunity have both been linked to DES. High blood glucose can trigger an inflammatory cascade that affects the overall function of the lacrimal gland and impairs the flow of normal oils from eyelid glands that keep tears from evaporating.

texts.orig: Like most diabetes complications, healthy blood glucose management and an A1C of less than 7 percent has been shown to help prevent diabetes-related eye complications like DES.

texts.orig: Treating DES
texts.text: Treating DES

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The treatment approach for DES depends largely on the severity and cause. Your treatment plan may also have to work around medications used for other health conditions that might be contributing to your DES. For example, you may need to continue taking beta-blockers to treat high blood pressure which is contributing to dryness in your eyes.
texts.text: The treatment approach for DES depends largely on the severity and cause. Your treatment plan may also have to work around medications used for other health conditions that might be contributing to your DES. For example, you may need to continue taking beta-blockers to treat high blood pressure which is contributing to dryness in your eyes.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: First, you'll need to work with your health care team to improve chronically high blood glucose (blood sugar). For some, this may help resolve your DES entirely.
texts.text: First, you'll need to work with your health care team to improve chronically high blood glucose (blood sugar). For some, this may help resolve your DES entirely.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Many people may need to begin using artificial tears daily to provide their eyes with adequate moisture.
texts.text: Many people may need to begin using artificial tears daily to provide their eyes with adequate moisture.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Your eye care team may recommend having your tear ducts blocked with silicone plugs or surgically closed to keep your tears in your eyes longer, giving them more time to moisten the surface of your eye.
texts.text: Your eye care team may recommend having your tear ducts blocked with silicone plugs or surgically closed to keep your tears in your eyes longer, giving them more time to moisten the surface of your eye.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Other common treatments include eye drop medications that increase tear production or low strength anti-inflammatory eye drops to help get the eyelid oil glands flowing normally, and even mechanical 'milking' of the oil glands to restore their normal function (home based devices or an in-office procedure).
